item.title: Expert Opinions About Hypnosis Have Shifted Over the Years
item.description:
Hypnosis

Expert Opinions About Hypnosis Have Shifted Over the Years

Is hypnosis a trance state or an instance of motivated role-playing?

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Early studies indicated that hypnosis could enable extraordinary feats.
  • Methodologically stronger studies have identified other explanations for the seeming specialness of hypnosis.
  • Most hypnotized persons are not simply faking. It's more complicated than that, psychologically.
  • Current thinking conceptualizes hypnosis as an instance of motivated role-playing.

In 1974, I was hypnotized as part of a stage show at the Celebrity Club in Hollywood, California. Miss Pat Collins, the beautiful Hip Hypnotist, moved a flame along my arm until my friends in the audience could smell the acrid odor of singed hair. Later in the show, Collins told me to become "stiff as a board" while her assistants placed me like a plank between two bar stools—and then she sat on my stomach!

Just before "waking me up," Collins told me I would remember nothing about what had happened. A few minutes later, when my friends asked me what I remembered, I said, "I don't remember anything." In fact, I remembered everything.

Early Studies of Hypnosis

In the 1950s and '60s, many studies supported the claim that hypnosis is an altered state of consciousness in which "special things" happen, things that do not and cannot happen in the normal waking state.

Two studies, for example, found that most hypnotized subjects will do dangerous things like pick up a rattlesnake or dip their hand into a beaker of acid (Rowland, 1939; Young, 1952).

Police departments learned that most eyewitnesses can recall additional details when hypnotized. The infamous Chowchilla kidnapping case of 26 children in 1976 was solved when bus driver Ed Ray, under hypnosis, recalled the license plate number of the kidnappers' van.

The late Ernest Hilgard, a highly regarded researcher at Stanford, demonstrated that highly hypnotizable subjects could immerse their arm in a tub of freezing water and report low levels of pain, much lower than when they were in a normal waking state (Hilgard, 1967). An obstetrician named R. V. August (1959) persuaded 295 women to give birth under hypnosis. Only 18 of the women eventually asked for a pain-killing drug.

Later Studies of Hypnosis

In the 1970s and '80s, better controlled studies cast doubt on the claim that hypnosis is a trance state in which special things happen. People discovered that the "extraordinary" feats performed in hypnosis stage shows are, in fact, easily done by someone sufficiently motivated. A moving flame is hot enough to singe arm hairs but not nearly hot enough to burn the skin. Almost anyone can become "stiff as a board" and suspended between bar stools.

Controlled studies have found that hypnotized subjects, as a group, perform no better than non-hypnotized subjects on standard memory tests (Steblay and Bouthwell, 1994). Eyewitnesses often recall additional details, not because of hypnosis per se but because the hypnotist uses memory techniques—observe the scene from different perspectives, zoom in, zoom out, roll the film back—that reliably produce higher levels of recall, even among individuals who are not hypnotized.

Other studies have found that hypnosis by itself does not reduce pain. In one study, volunteers reported low pain levels when they were told they would "feel no pain." Being hypnotized or not made no difference (Evans and Paul, 1970).

What about the hundreds of women who gave birth under hypnosis without pain-killing drugs? First, being relaxed (via hypnosis or other means) inhibits feelings of pain and anxiety. Second, the experience of pain is highly dependent on one's focus of attention. That's why injured soldiers and athletes often do not feel the pain of their injury until after the battle or game. Women who give birth under hypnosis are sometimes instructed to complete a task, like counting backwards by threes, that requires all of one's attention. Any distraction technique is an excellent way to minimize pain.

The Role-Playing Model of Hypnosis

If hypnosis is not a trance state, then what is it? Many researchers today believe that hypnosis is a loosely scripted interaction between two individuals—a hypnotist and a motivated subject—who act out an entertaining, sometimes dramatic story. Each person acts appropriately to their role, as learned from books, movies, TV shows, and stage shows.

Much evidence supports this new understanding of hypnosis. Individuals who like new roles and have some experience acting are generally better hypnotic subjects. People in other countries who have zero knowledge of the hypnosis "script" cannot be hypnotized (although they may be able to go into a believable voodoo trance). Volunteers led to believe that hypnosis induces hand paralysis (it doesn't) are likely to exhibit hand paralysis when hypnotized. For detailed discussions of hypnosis as a kind of motivated role-playing, see Spanos (1986) and Wenegrat (2001, chapter 4).

Are hypnotized subjects simply faking? Sometimes, but not always. It's more complicated than that, psychologically. When Miss Pat Collins hypnotized me, there was an unspoken agreement between us. I would do my part to help her create an entertaining stage show, and she would not ask me to do something truly embarrassing. After the show, I deceived my friends about what I remembered because (1) I wanted to honor that unspoken agreement and (2) I didn't want to besmirch the reputation of a beautiful woman who had allowed me to shine as a performer that evening.

item.title: Narcissism and Romantic Relationships: Repetition Compulsion
item.description:
Narcissism

Narcissism and Romantic Relationships: Repetition Compulsion

How narcissism hinders and undermines one's efforts to achieve intimacy.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Neurotic narcissism often undermines intimate relationships.
  • The repetition compulsion can play out in the therapy relationship as well.
  • Overcoming the repetition compulsion requires more than mere cognitive or intellectual insight.
Narcissus. Attributed to Frans de Neve
Source: Wikimedia Commons

This is Part 3 of a series on narcissism and romantic relationships.

In Part 1 and Part 2 of this series, we discussed different dynamics related to neurotic narcissism that tend to hinder and undermine romantic relationships. Indeed, one of the most common problems psychotherapists see is a chronic and repetitive pattern of dysfunctional relationships. And each relationship eventually ends badly because of these same dynamics.

Groundhog Day

This is very much like what happens to Bill Murray in the memorable film Groundhog Day (1993). Those who have seen it no doubt recall Murray’s starring role (Phil Connors) as a totally narcissistic, self-centered, egotistical television weather man. After a while, such negative attitudes and self-defeating patterns of behavior and narcissistic signs (see my prior post)—objectively obvious to others—slowly begin to become evident, even to the patient. (In Connors’ case, by dint of suddenly being bizarrely forced, as described in Nietzsche’s 1882 idea of “eternal recurrence,” to literally repeat the same day, same mundane details, and same interpersonal interactions over and over, ad nauseum.)

Nevertheless, the consistently selfish behavior with its predictable consequences commonly continues both for the narcissistic client and those attracted to them, as is typically the case with character disorders in general. The person is unable to help themselves from acting this way despite making conscious efforts to do so. And the inevitable question arises: Why? Why would anyone in their right mind persist in pursuing relationships that are obviously doomed to failure? What’s happening here?

The Profound Fear of Intimacy

There are no easy explanations for such persistent self-defeating behavior. One part of the puzzle has to do with a profound fear of intimacy. If we fear the opposite (or, for that matter, same) sex, how can we relate intimately to them? (On an archetypal level, there is what depth psychologists call “fear of the feminine” and “fear of the masculine” at play here.)

True intimacy makes one far too vulnerable to being hurt, rejected, abandoned, or betrayed, something that the narcissistic patient all-too-painfully experienced early in life, when what Kohut ( 1978 ) calls their “healthy” or normal narcissistic needs were, in one way or another, not adequately met. Instead, we defend ourselves from true intimacy with thorny defenses (see Part 2) that keep potentially dangerous others—and the anxiety they evoke—safely at arm’s length. And, since this is usually done quite unconsciously, it becomes a compulsive, repetitive pattern, undermining and sabotaging every close relationship we attempt to create. It is an excellent example of what Freud (1920) referred to as a “repetition compulsion.” And it is directly related to the problem of pathological narcissism but commonly occurs also in borderline personality disorder as well as some other psychiatric conditions.

What Is a Repetition Compulsion?

A repetition compulsion is, by definition, an unconscious neurotic defense mechanism. Here’s how it works. The repetition compulsion is a futile attempt to rewrite history and reality. The history we try to rewrite as adults is typically the troubled or inadequate relationship with our parents or primary caretakers, particularly the opposite sex parent: i.e., the origin of the narcissistic wounding.

When the early parental relationship is fraught with frustration, disappointment, rejection, abandonment, neglect, or abuse, it places the child in a precarious position psychologically. In order to survive these devastating so-called narcissistic insults, wounds, or injuries, children deny, dissociate, or minimize the painful reality of their predicament, repressing their feelings of anger, rage, depression, and despair. Instead, they hang on to hope: childish hope, a kind of “magical thinking” that, if only we can be as good, nice, perfect, polite, popular, smart, quiet, athletic, talented, successful, or amusing as we perceive our parents or caretakers wish us to be, we will eventually get them to love us as we—and every child—want and need them to. This is the childish fantasy that underlies and informs neurotic narcissism.

Sadly, in reality, this will never happen no matter what we do (or don’t do) because the problem actually lies with the parent’s incapacity to perfectly love and accept us as we are, bad behavior, neediness, dependency, and all. This misinterpretation of reality feeds into a child’s grandiose belief, what in CBT is called a “core schema,” that they possess the power to control and rectify the deficiency by transforming themselves into someone more acceptable and that there must be something terribly wrong with them, an inherent unlovability or unworthiness, an almost delusional “cognitive distortion” unconsciously carried into adulthood. And so, the narcissistic adult in the powerful clutches of the repetition compulsion (or perhaps more accurately stated, of their “inner child”) continues to try desperately to get the love they needed and deserved, only now from symbolic stand-ins for the parents. But to no avail. For no one now can undo what was done or provide what was unfortunately not provided during childhood.

The “Abandonment Depression”

Certainly, not even the best parents are perfect, and so we all go through this to some degree in one way or another. Just as our parents did. It is an existential fact of life. We can consider ourselves fortunate to have parents or caretakers who, though clearly flawed, were “good enough” to employ Winnicott’s (1953) term. In reality, this is tragically not always the case. Which makes the repetition compulsion and repressed abandonment depression even more powerful and potentially devastating. The emotional, and sometimes physical, abandonment has already long ago happened, and the child defended against it as best they could so as not to be destructively overwhelmed.

Part of that primitive defense mechanism includes the comprehensible hope of being able to change the parent’s response by becoming what we perceive they want us to become, which wards off what psychoanalyst James Masterson (1990) aptly terms the “abandonment depression.” So long as we continue to unconsciously cling to this childish hope, we avoid drowning in despair. A child is psychologically and developmentally unequipped to deal with such loss, but the adult patient has more resilience and inner and outer resources available to swallow this “bitter pill” and the accompanying emotions if they choose to in therapy.

In adulthood, this early childhood scenario is unconsciously and compulsively recapitulated by most of us to some degree or another. Our so-called “inner child” complex is active and still seeking to turn the rejecting, ambivalent, emotionally unavailable, or abusive adult into a loving one, despite having failed to do so during childhood. This becomes the primary sign, symptom, and signature of the patient’s problematic repetition compulsion, which plays out at times in the transference relationship with the therapist.

item.title: What a Jail Cell Taught Me About Broken Mental Health Care
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

What a Jail Cell Taught Me About Broken Mental Health Care

Personal Perspective: Our mental health system is containment, not compassion.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Our mental health system too often jails people with severe mental illness instead of treating them.
  • Because humans regulate one another's physiology, isolation is among the cruelest punishments we can inflict.
  • A system that leaves the sick to be saved by accident is offering containment, not treatment.
Source: Brett Sayles Pexels

The segregation cell, the jail's antiseptic name for solitary confinement, was about four feet by four feet. Beige brick, a red steel door, a six-inch window of scratched plexiglass that looked out on nothing. No horizon. No depth. For a man in the full grip of mania, it was close to unbearable. The air felt thin. My mind ricocheted off the walls.

On the first night, the claustrophobia rose toward panic, and I could not breathe. I tilted my head back toward the ceiling and caught it—a faint, cool draft from a vent above me: a thin current of moving air.

I turned my face up to it the way you turn toward a hand laid on your shoulder in the dark. And without warning, it brought me, my father. He had died a few months earlier, his body slowly stilled by Parkinson's, and as the draft moved over my skin I felt improbably close to him: two men worn to their most basic suffering, meeting in the plain fact of breath.

It was barely anything. It was everything.

That accidental breath of air was the first stillness I had known in weeks. It was not transcendence. It was just air. And it was enough to keep me from disappearing into the noise of my own mind.

I want to tell you how I got to that cell, because the smallness of that mercy is the whole point.

How I Ended Up in a Cell Instead of a Hospital

Days earlier, a clinician I will call M had declined to sign an emergency detention, the order that might have sent me to a hospital. I was floridly manic. I had sent my brothers messages I can still barely stand to describe. By any honest reading, I was a person who needed care.

But the question the system asks is not whether you are suffering; it is whether you are dangerous. On the metric of provable danger, I did not clear the bar, so there was no hospital bed—only booking, a uniform, a body scan, a holding cell.

I was booked in the grip of a manic psychotic episode, and the jail's own social worker saw it plainly. She asked about my history and named what she found: probable bipolar disorder, probable PTSD. She did not accuse. She recognized. The nurse who screened me confirmed I was breathing, confirmed I was a person, and she wrote it down.

None of it changed how I was handled. Moved to a dormitory, I asked deputy after deputy for food that never came. Mania turns hunger into injustice, and by midnight I was protesting too loudly to be ignored. For that, for the very symptom the social worker had just documented, I was escorted to solitary. My illness was recorded in one room and punished as non-compliance in the next.

To answer a disintegrating mind with isolation is to prescribe the one thing most likely to finish it off. In A General Theory of Love, the psychiatrists Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini, and Richard Lannon argue that because human beings regulate one another's physiology, expulsion from the company of others is the cruelest punishment we can devise. The jail's response to a man losing himself was to strip away the last thing that might have held him: Other people.

No medication came.

I was placed on suicide precautions and fitted with a padded green anti-suicide smock, a turtle suit in the inmates' slang. I said aloud that I was losing myself. And the only mercy that reached me came from none of the people paid to keep me alive. It came from the building's ventilation.

Source: Мансур Тляков/Pixabay

Containment Is Not Care

The draft did not heal me. It did not treat my bipolar disorder or shorten my episode by an hour. It was a mechanical accident in a room built to contain a body and wait.

But it did the one thing nothing else in that building did. It reached me. In a place built to keep a body still and leave a mind to burn, one small current refused to stay put. It moved. Because it moved, I could feel it. Because I could feel it, I was, for a few minutes, somewhere. Present. Here.

That is the distinction I keep returning to: What I received was contact, not comfort. It offered nothing that resembled care. It simply touched me, reminding a self I had nearly lost that a world still existed beyond my own mind. Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Elio Frattaroli writes that we discover who we are in our awareness of feeling, not thinking. In that cell, thinking had become the disease. The air gave me something to feel, a thin thread back to the world, and it held.

This was the exact measure of what the system offered me. Not care. Not treatment. Containment, and a small mercy it did not intend. In the New England Journal of Medicine, the psychiatrists Caleb Gardner and Arthur Kleinman named the pattern without flinching: modern psychiatry, they wrote, is marked by the "abandonment and incarceration of people with chronic, severe mental illness." I did not meet that sentence as a patient reading a journal. I lived it as an inmate. The jail was where the abandonment became a room.

Jails, as I wrote last time, have quietly become the country's largest psychiatric institutions. The journalist Alisa Roth calls this America's criminal treatment of mental illness, and I have no better words for it. This is how that abstraction feels from inside a cell: like being sick enough to be locked up and not sick enough to be helped. Like telling someone you are disappearing and being left alone to find out whether you will.

And it feels, on the first night, like tilting your face toward a vent and being kept in the world, for a few minutes, by moving air.

I got well, eventually. Not there, and not because of anything that place did. But I have never forgotten the smallest mercy, or how much it exposed by being the only one on offer. A person in psychiatric crisis should not have to be kept alive by the ductwork. That so many of us are—that our emergency care can amount to a locked door, a padded smock, and whatever grace the building's machinery happens to leak into the dark—tells us everything about the distance between confining a person and caring for one.

item.title: Raising Teens Who Choose Healthy Relationships
item.description:
Adolescence

Raising Teens Who Choose Healthy Relationships

How parents can build connection instead of controlling during dating years.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Preparing teens for healthy relationships begins years before they go on their first date.
  • Open, judgment-free conversations help teenagers recognize unhealthy relationship patterns.
  • A sense of self-worth is the most effective protective factor against unhealthy dating relationships.

Romantic relationships are an important part of adolescent development, yet they often leave parents feeling uncertain. One day you’re reminding your child to brush their teeth before bed, and the next they’re asking if they can go on their first date. It’s no surprise that many parents respond with anxiety. Concerns about heartbreak, peer pressure, social media, unhealthy relationships, and sex can make the dating years feel overwhelming.

Parents often ask, “What age should I let my teen date?” While there isn’t a universal answer to that question, it is the wrong question to be asking. Rather than focusing on when teenagers can date, we should be asking whether they have the emotional skills needed to build healthy relationships.

The truth is that dating itself isn’t the greatest risk. Entering relationships without the tools to recognize respect, communicate effectively, and establish healthy boundaries is.

Dating Readiness Is About Maturity, Not Age

There is no magic birthday that suddenly prepares a teenager for dating. Emotional maturity develops at different rates, and readiness depends on much more than age.

Before beginning a romantic relationship, teenagers benefit from developing several important life skills, including:

  • Communicating honestly and respectfully
  • Managing disappointment and conflict without aggression
  • Respecting their own boundaries and those of others
  • Balancing relationships with family, school, hobbies, and friendships
  • Feeling comfortable asking trusted adults for help when something doesn’t feel right

Parents often feel pressure to establish rigid rules about dating. While family expectations are important, helping teens develop sound judgment ultimately protects them far more than simply prohibiting relationships.

Healthy Relationships Begin Long Before the First Date

Many parents assume that dating skills develop once teenagers begin romantic relationships. Those lessons begin much earlier.

Children learn about relationships by watching the adults around them.

Every respectful disagreement they witness, every sincere apology they observe, and every healthy boundary they see modeled teaches them what loving relationships should look like. Even everyday interactions between parents, caregivers, siblings, and friends quietly shape a child’s expectations about how people should treat one another.

Long before teenagers begin dating, they are already developing beliefs about trust, communication, kindness, and respect.

Don’t Minimize Teenage Emotions

Adults sometimes dismiss adolescent relationships as “puppy love.” While these early romances may seem brief or insignificant from an adult perspective, they often feel incredibly meaningful to teenagers.

Developmentally, this makes sense.

During adolescence, the emotional centers of the brain mature earlier than the areas responsible for planning, judgment, and impulse control. As a result, teens often experience emotions with remarkable intensity.

When parents respond to heartbreak with comments like, “You’ll get over it,” or “It wasn’t that serious,” they may unintentionally communicate that their child’s emotions aren’t valid. Instead, try acknowledging the experience: “I know this really hurts.” “I’m glad you’re talking with me about it.”

Feeling understood doesn’t make heartbreak disappear, but it helps preserve one of the most valuable parts of the parent-child relationship: trust.

Curiosity Creates Better Conversations Than Criticism

Parents naturally want to protect their teenagers, particularly if they have concerns about a boyfriend or girlfriend. Unfortunately, criticism often has the opposite effect. When parents immediately attack a relationship, many teenagers become defensive and pull away. Curiosity opens far more doors than criticism. Instead of asking only questions that investigate the relationship, consider asking questions that encourage reflection:

  • What do you enjoy most about spending time with them?
  • How do you feel about yourself when you’re together?
  • Do you feel respected?
  • Do you feel comfortable sharing your opinions?
  • Do you feel more like yourself—or less like yourself—when you’re with them?

These conversations help teenagers begin evaluating relationships through their own experiences rather than simply reacting to parental opinions.

Teach Teens What Healthy Relationships Actually Look Like

Many teenagers receive surprisingly little direct instruction about healthy romantic relationships. Parents can help by discussing both positive qualities and warning signs.

Healthy relationships are characterized by:

  • Mutual respect
  • Honesty
  • Trust
  • Kindness
  • Support during difficult times
  • Healthy conflict resolution
  • Respect for personal boundaries

Parents should also discuss unhealthy behaviors that are sometimes mistaken for love, including:

  • Constant jealousy
  • Demanding passwords
  • Monitoring someone’s location
  • Requiring immediate replies to text messages
  • Isolating someone from friends or family
  • Insults disguised as humor
  • Pressuring someone into sexual activity
  • Any form of physical intimidation or violence

Controlling behavior is never a sign of love.

Dating Looks Different in the Digital Age

Today’s teenagers aren’t just dating in person—they’re also navigating relationships through text messages, social media, gaming platforms, and private messaging apps. Technology has created new challenges that previous generations never experienced.

Parents should have ongoing conversations about:

  • Digital privacy
  • Respectful online communication
  • Sexting
  • Consent
  • Sharing personal information
  • Healthy technology boundaries

Rather than relying on scare tactics, focus on helping teenagers understand that healthy relationships never require sacrificing privacy, comfort, or personal values to keep another person happy.

Healthy Self-Worth Is the Best Protection

Perhaps the greatest gift parents can give their teenagers is helping them develop a healthy sense of self-worth. Teenagers who believe they deserve kindness and respect are far less likely to tolerate manipulation, emotional abuse, or controlling relationships. Self-worth develops gradually through thousands of everyday interactions with caring adults who consistently communicate:

“You deserve to be treated with respect.”

“You never have to change who you are to earn someone’s love.”

“Healthy relationships should help you become more yourself—not less.”

Those messages often become the internal voice teenagers rely on when difficult relationship decisions arise.

Our Goal Isn’t to Prevent Dating—It’s to Prepare for It

No parent can eliminate every disappointment their teenager will experience. Heartbreak is painful. Conflict happens. Relationships sometimes end. But these experiences also provide opportunities for resilience, emotional growth, and self-discovery. Our job isn’t to control every relationship our teenagers enter.

Our job is to become the safe place they return to when relationships become confusing, painful, or complicated. When teenagers know they can come to us without fear of judgment, we remain one of the most powerful protective factors in their lives. And perhaps that’s the greatest lesson we can teach them: healthy relationships begin with knowing your own worth—and always having someone who reminds you of it.

item.title: Crossing the Finish Line When It Is Hard to Forgive
item.description:
Forgiveness

Crossing the Finish Line When It Is Hard to Forgive

Don't be discouraged if you have tried and have not yet forgiven. You can win.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Science shows that when we forgive, this can reduce nagging resentment and help people have more inner peace.
  • Sometimes, as people begin to forgive someone who acted unjustly, they run into difficulty completing it.
  • These methods may aid your forgiveness process, helping you cross the finish line of forgiveness.

Diane was patient with her boss as he made unrealistic demands that put her under pressure. She tried to show him that his timelines for completing work were unrealistic, but his demands persisted. She eventually switched jobs to a new company. In the process, she began to forgive her past boss. One of her motivations was her awareness that scientific studies show that as people forgive, they can significantly reduce their resentment. As she practiced forgiveness, she was surprised to continually “run into roadblocks.” In her desire to keep trying forgiveness, she attempted the five approaches I suggested earlier. Yet, she asked for more approaches to forgive.

If you share this same difficulty in forgiving, below are seven more ways to help you confront the injustices you have faced, forgive the person deeply and well, and move on from the inner discontent that may have been nagging you for a long time.

Source: Andrey Kekyalyaynen / Dreamstime

1. Small steps are better than giant steps as you practice patience. Do not expect too much progress too fast. It takes the moral virtue of patience to cross the finish line of forgiveness. In our hurry-up world, we expect instant results, yet forgiving takes time. Pause and see the other’s inner woundedness, not to excuse, but instead to start seeing the full humanity in the other. Diane went back in her mind to the boss's continual unhappiness. Was he miserable in his job, and was he passing that on to others? Did his parents have unrealistic expectations of him, and so he grew up with the wrong way of dealing with others? Take your time seeing the one who hurt you, with a fuller view of who the person is. Are you aware of any suffering this person endured in their younger years?

2. Cultivate a strong will. What is your usual pattern in life? Do you sometimes start projects, but do not complete them? Is this a regular occurrence for you? If so, recall at least three situations in which you persevered, despite difficulty, and finished the task. Now apply that to your forgiveness. You have completed tasks in the past, and so apply that tenacity to the current forgiveness project.

3. Practice bearing the pain in challenging areas that are not about forgiving. An important part of forgiveness is learning to “bear the pain” for the one who hurt you so that you do not displace that pain onto innocent and unsuspecting others. You can practice bearing pain outside the context of forgiveness. For example, if you are driving your car and in a hurry, you might get irritated by slow traffic. Think of this as a good chance to practice staying calm and rolling with what's happening so you don't get as easily annoyed. You can learn this patience when in emotional pain, then transfer the learning to the forgiveness process toward the one who is hard to forgive.

4. Draw inspiration from forgiveness heroes. We have many forgiveness heroes who might inspire you. Martin Luther King, Jr. wrote a book, Strength to Love, encouraging readers to forgive. He wrote this at a time when his family was under threat, and yet he stood firm in his resolve to love. Holocaust survivor Corrie Ten Boom forgave the SS officer who was abusive to her when she was imprisoned. He approached her one day after she gave a forgiveness talk, and he asked for forgiveness, which she granted. These heroes model forgiveness for us and can be inspiring as we complete the task.

Source: Walter Arce / Dreamstime

5. Shift your focus from healing yourself to doing good for the person who was cruel to you. It is good to have a motive to help yourself in forgiving. As an analogy, if you hurt your knee, it is good to focus on yourself and seek medical help to heal. It is the same with forgiveness; however, there are more motivations for forgiveness than an exclusive self-focus. If you begin to cultivate mercy toward the other, with a motivation that this person lead a fair life, this can slowly start to change your heart toward greater forgiveness for this person.

6. Work on finding meaning in suffering. Viktor Frankl, in his classic work, Man’s Search for Meaning, discusses how his standing in the truth of the grave injustices of his imprisonment strengthened his ability to see the truth. He grew in his suffering by finding meaning in the fact that he was growing in his understanding of the truth of justice while his captors were degenerating in it. Are you becoming more sensitive to the suffering of others as you suffer? See if this is the case. If it is, acknowledge your suffering is not for nothing. You are growing in your humanity as you suffer and forgive.

7. Practice on an easier case in which you are not as resentful. The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle emphasized practice when exercising any of the moral virtues. If you can start to forgive a person who was not very hurtful to you, then you become more familiar with the forgiveness process, possibly grow in confidence with this process, and even learn to embrace this virtue as part of your life. You then can take this newfound improvement in forgiving and apply it to the one who is hard to forgive.

In the long run, if you take the small steps first, cultivate the strong will, bear pain in various life circumstances, shift your compassion toward the one who hurt you, as Corrie Ten Boom did, find meaning in your suffering, and try practicing forgiveness on others first, you may find triumph in your forgiving as you cross the forgiveness finish line. Even then, you may have to revisit forgiving in the hard cases because the anger, although reduced, may remain to a small degree.

Source: Photographerlondon / Dreamstime

item.title: How Does AI Make You Feel?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How Does AI Make You Feel?

Four steps to monitor the influence our AI tools have on our bodies and minds

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • AI interactions can trigger bodily responses, such as physical tension and dopamine bursts.
  • Some people form emotional bonds with AI, but overuse is linked to anxiety, technostress, and "brain fry."
  • Individual AI habits ripple into families and society, making agency decay a social crisis.
Human existence is multidimensional. Every experience is influenced by our internal dimensions. AI is now influencing that dynamic from the outside in.
Source: AI-Generated / ChatGPT / 2026

Something registers in the body and in the mood well before we consciously decide whether an exchange with an AI system went well. Do you feel your shoulders tighten when a bot answers with delay? Do you feel relief spreading through your chest when, unexpectedly, a couple of prompts solved a hard problem smoothly? Does your heartbeat accelerate during an intensive “conversation” you’re having with your chatbot? These reactions are part of the texture that characterizes our hybrid relationships.

Four Dimensions, One Experience

Aspirations pull us toward what matters. Emotion tints the pulling. The mind sorts, plans, and doubts. Sensation registers the whole event in muscle, gut, skin. These four arrive together, each shaping the others, and any accurate account of what AI does to a person has to move through all four, because AI touches all four, while being influenced in return by how the user expresses them externally.

We are part of an organically evolving, hybrid kaleidoscope—and that dynamic is part of us. Let’s go through the four internal dimensions one by one:

The Body’s Response

Sensation is where the reaction starts, often before the mind catches up. Researchers studying interoception, the sense of one’s own heartbeat, breath, and gut, have built a decade-long case that cognition and internal bodily signals cannot be pulled apart. A judgment about a chatbot’s tone, a recommendation, an unexpected answer, rides partly on the internal dynamic underneath it.

The reward built into many AI-driven tools compounds this. Harvard Health describes how the small hit attached to a fast, flattering, or surprising response produces a measurable dopamine surge, the same chemical messenger tangled up in every craving. A newer measurement tool built specifically for this territory, the AI Fatigue Scale, confirms a physical dimension to sustained AI use distinct from the cognitive and emotional strain layered on top of it: tension, tiredness, and a kind of bodily bracing that accumulates across a day of AI-assisted work.

The Heart’s Response

Emotionally, the picture splits in at least two directions. On one side, comfort and even excitement: AI companions and assistants offer responsiveness without the friction, unpredictability, or unavailability that shape most human relationships. More and more studies in this territory describe real emotional bonds forming between people and systems built never to disagree, tire, or leave.

On the other side, a growing body of research links heavy or uncertain AI use to anxiety and low mood. A 2025 analysis found that technostress from rapid AI integration correlates with heightened anxiety and depressive symptoms, driven by the uncertainty, loss of control, and cognitive overload that can accompany constant exposure to AI-driven systems. The same exhaustion shows up plainly in workplace settings, where employees describe a specific, recognizable tiredness tied to keeping pace with tools that keep changing under them. Especially users interacting with agentic AI report “brain fry”—a dizzying experience that is both exciting and tiring.

The Mind’s Response

Thought carries its own weight. A national survey conducted this year found that most Americans expect AI to weaken both creative thinking and the capacity to form meaningful relationships. A much smaller share expects either faculty to improve.

That expectation shapes behavior on its own terms: a mind convinced in advance that a tool will dull it approaches that tool differently than a mind that trusts itself to stay in the loop. Confidence, in this sense, shapes the very faculty it worries about losing. Those who trust their AI more than their NI—their natural intelligence—are those who are most at risk of over-relying on the former, further jeopardizing their natural assets.

The Undercurrent: Aspiration

Aspiration is the hardest of the four to capture in a survey question, and the slowest to surface in the hybrid landscape. What do you aspire to, if everything that you have ever dreamt to accomplish can already, or likely will soon, be done by an artificial tool? What do you strive for now? What do you want now that software can draft that email, plan the trip, draw that painting that you had in the back of your head?

The previous answer, that a person wants whatever a machine cannot do, no longer holds with much confidence. At work, where purpose is supposed to be sturdy, about half of employees describe feeling worried about how AI will reshape their role; roughly a third describe feeling hopeful about the same shift. The gap where purpose used to sit by default now needs deliberate filling. If you never thought about your why, now is the time to start.

Systems, Not Layers

None of this stays private to one body. What happens at the individual level, the micro dimension, ripples into families and teams, the meso layer, into institutions and markets, the macro layer, and eventually into the wider fabric of shared life, the meta layer. A single person’s rising dependence on an AI companion is a micro event with meso consequences for a household and macro consequences for a whole generation’s baseline expectation of connection. These dimensions behave like weather systems, feeding each other constantly, indifferent to the tidy separations drawn between them on paper.

Agency decay amid AI: our gradually growing addiction to artificial intelligence is not only a personal issue, but also a social emergency, and the window to do something about it is closing. Fast.

Four Steps, One Word

Attention, applied consciously across all four dimensions, is one grounding move available to anyone navigating this terrain. Take these four steps, which are gathered under one word (useful for remembering): POZE.

Pause before the next tap, the next prompt, the next reflexive reach for a device. A single breath is enough to let sensation catch up with intention.

Observe what is actually happening in the body and the mood in that moment, without editing the report on the way in. Curiosity beats judgment here, every time.

Zoom in on the one relationship, one task, one thought that matters most right now, instead of the dozen competing for a slice of it.

Experience the moment fully, device present or absent, because presence is the one output no algorithm can generate on a person’s behalf.

AI will keep touching every one of our four dimensions, invited or not. We can protect them, starting from the inside out.
